classification.difficultyReason: Simplify the supplied recurrence and solve its quadratic, then transfer the repeating-tail idea to the new fraction in part c and select positive roots consistent with the definitions.

content.prompt:
A number, $x$, is defined by:
$$x=\cfrac{1}{2+\cfrac{1}{3+\cfrac{1}{2+\cfrac{1}{3+\cdots}}}}$$
where the dots indicate that the pattern continues forever.

children.label: a
children.prompt: As the pattern repeats indefinitely, we can write $x=\dfrac{1}{2+\dfrac{1}{3+x}}$. Simplify this to give a quadratic equation for $x$.

answer.short:
The quadratic has roots $\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{15}}{2}$.

The continued fraction is positive, so $x=\dfrac{-3+\sqrt{15}}{2}$.
answer.worked:
For $2x^2+6x-3=0$, the discriminant is
$$\begin{align*}b^2-4ac&=6^2-4(2)(-3)\\b^2-4ac&=60.\end{align*}$$
Thus
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{-6\pm\sqrt{60}}{4}\\x&=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{align*}$$
Every denominator in the defining continued fraction is positive, so its value is positive. Hence $x=\dfrac{-3+\sqrt{15}}{2}$.

answer.short:
$y=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt5}{2}$.

Use the repeating tail to write $y=\dfrac{1}{1+y}$ and take the positive root.
answer.worked:
The repeating tail has value $y$, so
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{1}{1+y}\\y(1+y)&=1\\y^2+y-1&=0.\end{align*}$$
The quadratic formula gives
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1^2-4(1)(-1)}}{2}\\y&=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{2}.\end{align*}$$
The continued fraction is positive, so $y=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt5}{2}$.
